Genghis Khan. Born Temujin, he was the founder and first great khan of the Mongol Empire, the largest contiguous land empire in history. Rising from obscurity among the nomadic tribes of the Gobi Desert, he unified the fragmented Mongol peoples and conquered vast territories from China to the steppes of Central Asia. His military innovations and organizational genius transformed a confederation of horse archers into the most formidable military force of the thirteenth century.

Genghis Khan was born around 1162 as a member of a minor Mongol clan. He took the name Temujin and gradually consolidated power through military prowess and political maneuvering. He united the feuding Mongol tribes under a single banner by the early twelve hundreds, taking the title Genghis Khan, meaning Universal Ruler, around 1206. He pioneered a military meritocracy that promoted soldiers based on ability rather than birth, revolutionizing warfare on the steppes and beyond.

He conquered vast territories across Asia, creating an empire that stretched from the Pacific to the edge of Europe. He established the Mongol Empire, which his son and successors expanded further. His grandson Kublai Khan founded the Yuan Dynasty in China. Genghis Khan employed devastating siege warfare, psychological warfare, and rapid cavalry tactics that overwhelmed settled civilizations unprepared for nomadic military methods. He codified the Yassa, an early legal code that unified Mongol practices and applied harsh discipline to his armies and conquered territories. He used intelligence networks and espionage extensively, gathering information on enemies before engaging them militarily. He died in 1227, likely from battle wounds or illness, and his empire was divided among his sons but remained loosely unified under successive great khans for over a century.
